new_statements.quote: In Kɔɖa the stress is not phonemic. Primary stress falls on the last syllable of the phonological word, where a phonological word is minimally bimoraic. A secondary stress typically falls on every second syllable preceding the syllable with the primary stress. A clitic does not get stressed unless it attaches to a monosyllabic root to create a disyllabic word. Vowels with a primary stress have a higher pitch than the other vowels and there is perceptive lengthening of stressed vowels. [...] (p. 12:) In Kɔɖa, stress falls on the final syllable of a phonological word irrespective of syllable weight

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive, predictable word stress: primary stress on the final syllable of the phonological word regardless of syllable weight (aˈgu 'bring', t̪ɔrˈhɔt 'monitor lizard', ˌkukuˈmu 'dream'); monosyllabic CV words lengthen to satisfy a bimoraic minimum (ˈmu: 'nose'); an enclitic attached to a monosyllabic root takes the final stress ([ɟomˈiŋ] 'I will eat'), otherwise clitics are unstressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress 'typically falls on every second syllable preceding the syllable with the primary stress' (alternating leftward), e.g. ˌʃɛnd̪ɛˈra 'hunting', ˌpɛnd̪ɛˈla 'lie', ˌkukuˈmu 'dream'.
new_statements.exceptions: Clitics are unstressed unless they attach to a monosyllabic root forming a disyllabic phonological word (then the clitic bears the final stress, p. 69). Medial unstressed open-syllable vowels in trisyllables are shortened/centralized ([ˌʃɛndəˈra]) or deleted in sequences of open syllables (/ci-lɛka/ -> cilka 'how'). No lexical exceptions listed; p. 24 hedges with 'typically'.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (root plus clitic can form one p-word; minimal word bimoraic). Author elicited stress data in a carrier phrase aiʔ X Kɔɖarɛ gamiʔtɛ 'He says X in Kɔɖa' and inspected F0/amplitude/duration in Praat; correlates named are higher pitch and lengthening. Described variety: Kɔɖa of Rajshahi region, north-west Bangladesh.
new_statements.identity_note: Shamim 2021 describes Kɔɖa as spoken in the Rajshahi region of north-west Bangladesh (the Glottolog koda1236 language-level entry; ISO cdz); he shows it closely matches Konow's 1906 Birbhum Koda. Senkuttuvan 2011 describes Koda/Kora of Midnapore district, West Bengal, India (same glottocode, different locale) and is silent on stress. Note Konow/Senkuttuvan warn that 'Koda/Kora' census returns elsewhere (Orissa, MP) may cover a Kurukh-like Dravidian variety, which is not this language.

sources.note: Section 2.4 'Stress' (pp. 67-69): stress not phonemic; primary stress on the last syllable of the phonological word (minimally bimoraic); secondary stress on every second syllable preceding the primary; clitics unstressed unless they complete a disyllabic word with a monosyllabic root; stressed vowels have higher pitch and are perceptibly lengthened; Table 2-5 gives ˈul, aˈgu, baˈga, t̪ɔrˈhɔt, ˌkukuˈmu, ˌʃɛnd̪ɛˈra. Typological sketch p. 11-12: final stress 'irrespective of syllable weight'; p. 24: 'stress is predictable, not contrastive... primary stress typically falls on the final syllable…

sources.note: Silent on stress. Phonology (pp. 434 ff.) lists 5 vowels, 24 consonants and only two 'Supra Segmental features': length /:/ and nasalization /~/; no mention of stress or accent anywhere in the chapter (data from Midnapore district, West Bengal).
